common_name: San Piero Fig (Teardrop Purple Italian Fig)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; San Piero is a vigorous, heavy-bearing Italian heirloom fig well suited to the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season.

directions: San Piero is a vigorous heirloom Italian fig, also grown under the synonym names Turkish Brown and Negro Largo, prized for its medium-to-large teardrop-shaped fruit with deep purple skin and richly sweet, strawberry-pink flesh. As a common-type fig it sets a reliable crop without pollination, typically producing a light early-summer breba crop and a heavier late-summer main crop. The tree is notably vigorous and productive, reaching 15-25 feet if left unpruned, but responds well to hard annual pruning to keep it manageable in home orchards and containers. San Piero tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity well and is closely related to the fig widely sold in warm-climate nurseries as 'Brown Turkey', sharing much of that cultivar's toughness and reliability.

common_name: Ventura Strawberry Fig (Adriatic-Type Red-Fleshed California Fig)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in full sun with excellent drainage; this Adriatic-type California selection is grown for its deep red, berry-flavored flesh and performs well in hot, sunny Gulf Coast conditions.

directions: Ventura Strawberry is a California selection within the Adriatic group of fig cultivars, named for the deep red, berry-like color and flavor of its flesh rather than for any trait of its skin. Fruits are medium-sized with dark purple-black skin and a thick, juicy, red interior that carries a distinct strawberry-like sweetness; as with other Adriatic types it sets a dependable main crop without needing pollination. The tree performs well in hot, sunny conditions and has become a sought-after specialty selection among Southern fig collectors for its rich flavor and productivity. Grow it as you would other common-type figs, in full sun with excellent drainage, and expect the first fruit within two to three years of planting a rooted cutting.

common_name: Angelique Fig (Early Yellow French Heirloom Fig)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Angelique is a centuries-old French heirloom valued for ripening earlier than most fig cultivars, giving Gulf Coast growers a crop before peak-summer humidity promotes splitting in later varieties.

directions: Angelique is a centuries-old French heirloom fig, historically grown around Paris and known there as Angelique or Melette, that Thomas Jefferson brought to Monticello after seeing it cultivated abroad. It bears medium to large fruit with pale greenish-yellow, subtly striped skin and sweet, cream-colored flesh, ripening notably early in the season and extending the fig harvest before later-season cultivars come in. As a common-type fig it is self-fertile and produces without pollination, and its long history of wide cultivation across France attests to its adaptability across a range of soils and climates. In the Gulf South, Angelique's early ripening window helps growers bring in a crop ahead of the peak summer humidity that promotes fruit souring and splitting in later-maturing varieties.

common_name: Garretson American Persimmon (Early Golden Seedling Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in full sun in any well-drained to average soil; Garretson is a seedling selection of 'Early Golden' valued for its large, sweet fruit and reliable production.

directions: Garretson is a named selection of the native American persimmon, raised as a seedling of the well-known 'Early Golden' cultivar and valued for its large, deep-orange, richly sweet fruit. Like most American persimmon selections it is primarily pistillate (female), so fruit set is heaviest when a seedling or named male tree is planted within pollinating range, though occasional male flowers on some branches can allow limited fruit set on their own. Fruit ripens in early October and, like all American persimmons, needs to fully soften after frost before it loses its mouth-puckering astringency and becomes honey-sweet. Garretson is cold-hardy into zone 4 and, thanks to the species' deep taproot and tolerance of heat, humidity, and poor soils, also thrives through the Gulf Coast's long, hot growing season.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in full sun in moist to well-drained soil; Killen is self-fruitful, so a single tree can set a crop without a separate pollinator nearby.

directions: Killen is a named native persimmon selection valued for its exceptionally sweet, blemish-free orange fruit and its self-fruitful habit, meaning a single tree can set a crop without a separate pollinator planted nearby. It is a somewhat smaller-statured American persimmon, typically maturing around 25 feet, which makes it easier to fit and harvest in a home orchard than many seedling-grown native persimmons. Like other Diospyros virginiana selections, Killen fruit remains firm and astringent until fully ripened and softened by autumn frosts, after which it turns rich, sweet, and custard-like. The tree is drought-tolerant once established, adaptable to a wide range of soil types, and well suited to the long, humid growing season of the Gulf Coast.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Collier Mulberry (Early-Ripening Large-Fruited Red Mulberry Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Collier is a cold-hardy red mulberry x white mulberry hybrid selection prized for its large fruit and early, concentrated harvest.

directions: Collier is a natural hybrid selection between red mulberry (Morus rubra) and white mulberry (Morus alba), chosen for its large fruit — up to two and a half inches long — and heavy, reliable production. It closely resembles the popular 'Illinois Everbearing' mulberry but ripens about two weeks earlier and concentrates its fruit set into a shorter, more manageable harvest window rather than trickling in over many weeks. Collier is markedly cold-hardy, tolerating winters well into the northern half of the country, which also gives it plenty of margin for the mild winters and long, hot growing season of Gulf Coast gardens. As with other mulberries, site female-fruiting trees away from patios, walkways, and parked cars, since the ripe, juicy berries drop over an extended period and stain hard surfaces.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
